BREAKING: Japanese banks sold -$16 billion of foreign bonds in September, their largest monthly sale since February.

This also marks their 9th consecutive monthly sale, the longest streak since 2022.

As a result, sales of foreign debt by Japanese banks in the first 9 months of 2026 were the largest for that period since 2005.

Japanese financial institutions have turned to domestic government bonds, whose yields have surged to their highest levels in 3 decades.

Over the 5 months ending in August, large banks and insurers bought +$34 billion of Japanese government bonds with maturities of 2 years or more, their largest 5-month purchase since the start of 2023.

Global bond demand is undergoing a historic shift as yields rise.

$PLTR More Maven action:

Maven is the backbone of NATO’s Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative:

“Command posts utilized next-generation command-and-control software, including the Maven Smart System, to establish a unified common operating picture across dispersed national headquarters. This common data backbone enabled military planners to process vast amounts of operational data, accelerate commander decision cycles and coordinate deep fires across the land, air, sea, cyber and space domains.”

“Conducted from Oct. 6 to 15, the exercise brought together approximately 2,000 U.S. service members and 2,000 multinational personnel operating from command posts across France, Germany, the Netherlands and Poland. Avenger Triad 26 was synchronized with NATO’s premier command post exercise, Steadfast Duel 26, which linked strategic and operational decision-makers across all 32 Allied nations.”

“A central objective of the exercise was putting concepts from NATO’s Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative into operational practice. Rather than relying solely on static lines of defense, EFDI integrates advanced sensors, unmanned aerial systems, cloud computing and shared data environments to shorten the time between threat detection and target engagement.”

“Last year we finished at a high level, and this year we started at that level,” Lowin said. “The credibility of our deterrence rests on our capability. When an adversary sees that 32 nations can share data seamlessly, command corps-level formations across thousands of kilometers and coordinate joint fires in minutes, it sends an unmistakable signal: attacking NATO will not succeed.”

Global smartphone purchases have collapsed.

Worldwide smartphone shipments dropped -22.0% YoY in Q3 2026, to 255.3 million units, their largest quarterly decline on record.

Samsung's shipments fell -5.8% YoY, to 57.8 million units, while Apple's declined -4.0% to 57.3 million units.

At the same time, Xiaomi shipments fell -29.2% YoY to 30.7 million units, Oppo dropped -34.5%, to 25.6 million units, while Vivo fell -31.5%, to 19.1 million units.

This comes as memory costs have surged +350% since last year, driven by AI-related demand, putting further pressure on smartphone manufacturers.

As a result, soaring component costs are forcing vendors to raise prices and reduce budget-focused offerings, with consumers increasingly keeping their existing devices for longer.

Global smartphone sales are contracting amid surging prices.

Andrew Moss, CMT@Andy__Moss
02:41 SGTInvesting
It’s about balance and being able to let the trade work.

Pyramiding is great. It’s also harder to do as it has a tendency to magnify discomfort.

If you can take full size, let the trade breathe, and watch it play out till the end, fantastic! Bigger for longer is obviously optimal for trades that are working.

But, if you get antsy when it starts to pullback, thinking about giving back profits, then trimming and trailing is a great method for alleviating that.

Like everything in trading it takes intense discipline. And that’s after you test different methods to find out what suits your mentality best.

Trading around a core is also a good approach. I have no problem adding back to a position if it sets up again with good r/r.

Jack Prescott@JackPrescottX
23:27 SGT quoteInvesting
AbCellera’s access to a top tier talent pool in their own backyard is an underappreciated asset that doesn’t show up on the balance sheet.

This passage from Zero to One is over 10 years old, but I believe it is still applicable today.

“Researchers experiment with things that just might work instead of refining definite theories about how the body's systems operate. Biologists say they need to work this way because the underlying biology is hard. According to them, IT startups work because we created computers ourselves and designed them to reliably obey our commands. Biotech is difficult because we didn't design our bodies, and the more we learn about them, the more complex they turn out to be.”

As it pertains to “instead of refining definite theories about how the body’s systems operate”, I am reminded of how the properties of a CD3 binding arm can change depending of the tumor binding arm it’s paired with in a bispecific. Mother Nature is indefinite and you must have the tools to navigate that. Of course, AbCellera seems to have proved they can with their diverse panels of binders and matrices used to define their panels of CD3 binders and optimal pairing: x.com/jackprescottx/…

Now, going after biology that has already been validated in some ways, such as NK3R with ABCL635 is an effective way to not be completely in the dark. Indefinite and definite is a spectrum IMO.

But at the end of the day, doing good science is paramount to success. You need elite minds with good judgement to know what targets are worth pursuing, how the studies should be designed, etc.

“experiment with things that just might work”… You need people with the intuition to know what might just work.

See Booth’s comments in the quoted post below regarding the talent pool AbCellera has access to. Again, this is an under appreciated asset.

$ABCL
Jack Prescott @JackPrescottX · 1 Jun 2025, 06:18 SGT
(2023) @AbCelleraBio CFO Andrew Booth highlights the strong talent in Vancouver:

“We find ourselves down in the United States at events and conferences and you realize 50% of the room is actually Canadians who have gone down and are living in Boston or in San Francisco. Actually, it's very difficult to start a company in Boston or San Francisco because the war for talent between all of the other companies that are starting to be there. In many ways the talent we have here in Vancouver is a a massive competitive advantage and what we need are great companies that can give them meaningful jobs to allow them to pursue a career in science and engineering.”

For perspective, total receipts rose just +3.2% YoY, to $5.40 trillion.

In other words, interest on federal debt accounted for 25% of total US government receipts.

Meanwhile, Social Security, the largest government expense, jumped +$86 billion YoY, or +5.5%, to a record $1.67 trillion.

At this pace, interest costs will exceed Social Security as the largest government outlay by the end of 2028.

The current market weakness does not surprise me at all.

Back in early-September, risk:reward was highly unfavourable if you considered the many macro hurdles I mentioned in my initial post + adverse flow data.

We also saw a slight relief rally in various AI names, driven by low vol/low conviction buys that meant tech was the "most" net-bought sector for around 5 weeks on the trot.

At this point, buying into strength / flow reversals seems to be the most prudent course of action. In other words, let HFs build positions back with some conviction first.

Q3 earnings may very well be that catalyst. Although mediocre reactions to ASML/TSMC earnings tells me otherwise, especially if we remain risk-off into next week which is when earnings really kick-off.

Given that there's now way more room for risk to be added, I still hold my view that we see a rally post-midterms, compounded by favourable earnings across the AI complex.

If you care about biotech and drug development watch this interview with Matt Gline, the CEO of Roivant, a biotech firm that is now worth $24 billion.

He talks about why he thinks predictions about AI from people like Anthropic’s Dario Amodei are overly optimistic.

“If Dario is right and I'm wrong, and he cures every disease in five years, man, are we all the winners from that outcome,” Gline said.

“I think if you work in this industry, it is very hard not to be skeptical of any of those claims. Because, and I've said this in other settings recently too, biotech is a wood chipper that like is built to like ingest souls and shred them. It's just like such a hard business that like someone comes and they're like, oh, but I've built a computer and I'm going to push a button and all of that goes away and it just works. Like that is probably not the way that's going to go.”

interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works
